INSTRUCTIONS¶

Complete the following questions individually using the provided data set. When prompted, fill out the cells with your code (in code cells) or text (in text cells) to answer the question. Part 1: The Data (2 points)¶

We will be exploring a data set on Women's March Madness (Basketball). This adapted data set contains historical records of every NCAA Division I Women’s Basketball Tournament appearance since the tournament began in 1982 up until 2018. Sourced from official NCAA, the adapted data set captures tournament results across more than four decades of collegiate women’s basketball. All data is sourced from the NCAA and contains the data behind the story The Rise and Fall Of Women’s NCAA Tournament Dynasties.

The data set can be read in from the following url: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/diverse-data-hub/diversedata/refs/heads/main/data-clean/womensmarchmadness.csv

To help you with the analysis, here is a table of descriptions of each of the variables present in the model.

Variable Description
year Year
school School Name
seed Seed. The 0 seeding designation in 1983 notes the eight teams that played an opening-round game to become the No. 8 seed in each region.
conference Conference
conf_wins Conference Wins
conf_losses Conference Losses
conf_wins_pct Conference Win Percentage
conf_rank Place in Conference
division Conference Division
reg_wins Regional Wins
reg_losses Regional Losses
reg_wins_pct Regional Win Percentage
bid Whether the school qualified with an automatic bid (by winning its conference or conference tournament) or an at-large bid. [‘at-large’, ‘auto’]
first_game_at_home Whether the school played its first-round tournament games on its home court. [‘Y’, ‘N’]
tourney_wins Tourney Wins
tourney_losses Tourney Losses
tourney_finish Ordered categories: [‘opening_round_loss’ < ‘first_round_loss’ < ‘second_round_loss’ < ‘top_16_loss’ < ‘top_8_loss’ < ‘top_4_loss’ < ‘top_2_loss’ < ‘champ’]
total_wins Total Wins
total_losses Total Losses
total_wins_pct Total Win Percentage

Task 5.1 Plan out your analysis (10 points)¶

Propose a method that was covered in class that would be appropriate to use to answer your research question. You only need to build one model with one set of predictors in this section. Write a paragraph that explains the choice of method, and be sure to answer the following questions:

  • What method do you plan to use?
  • Why is this method appropriate?
  • What are the potential limitations or weaknesses of the method selected?
  • How are you going to process the data to apply the model? For example: Are you splitting the data? How? How many splits? What proportions will you use for the splits? At what stage will you split? Will there be a validation set? Will you use cross validation?
  • How will you assess the performance of the model? Explain why the performance metric(s) chosen ise appropriate.

You answer should be around 250 words or less.

I plan to use KNN classification to predict tournament finish using seed and conference win percentage. KNN is appropriate because the outcome is categorical, and it predicts outcomes using teams with similar predictor values. Its limitaions include sensitivity to vairiable scales and the choice may also lead to poor predictions for rare outcomes, and 2 predictors may not capture all relevant information. Before imputaions or standardization ,I will randomly spilt the data into 75% training and 25% testing. I will use five_fold cross_validation within the training set to select K based on mean validation accuracy, without a seperate validation within the training set to select K based on mean validation accuracy, without a seperate validation set. Within each fold, missing win percentage will be filled using the training portion's mean, and both predictors will be standardized using that portion's statistics. After choosing K, I will fit the workflow on the full training set and evaluate it once on the test set. I will use accuracy to measure the proportion of correct predictions and a confusion matrix to examine errors across categories. Because the categories are imbalenced, I will also compare accuracy with a baseline that always predicts the most common training-set category

Task 5.2 Perform the Analysis (20 points)¶

  • Perform the proposed analysis.
  • Be sure to comment your code throughout so that it is easy to follow.

You may add more code cells if needed.

In [43]:
### EDIT THIS CODE CELL ###
library(tidymodels)
library(tidyverse)

# Make the random split reproducible.
set.seed(123)

# Split the data before imputaion and standardization.
basketball_split <- initial_split(basketball_tidy, prop = 0.75)
basketball_train <- training(basketball_split)
basketball_test <- testing(basketball_split)

# Create five folds using only the training data.
basketball_folds <- vfold_cv(basketball_train, v = 5)
In [44]:
# Replace missing predictor values with training means,
# then center and scale both numeric predictors.
basketball_recipe <- recipe(
    tourney_finish ~ seed + conf_wins_pct,
    data = basketball_train
) |>
    step_impute_mean(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
    step_center(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
    step_scale(all_numeric_predictors())

# Tune the number of neighbor using cross-validation.
knn_spec <- nearest_neighbor(
    weight_func = "rectangular",
    neighbors = tune()
) |>
    set_engine("kknn") |>
    set_mode("classification")

# Combine preprocessing and the model.
basketball_workflow <- workflow() |>
    add_recipe(basketball_recipe) |>
    add_model(knn_spec)
In [45]:
# Compare odd K values from 1 to 31.
k_grid <- tibble(neighbors = seq(1, 31, by = 2))
set.seed(123)

# Evaluate each K using mean validation accuracy.
basketball_tuning <- basketball_workflow |>
    tune_grid(
        resamples = basketball_folds,
        grid = k_grid,
        metrics = metric_set(accuracy)
    )

# Display cross-validation results.
basketball_cv_results <- collect_metrics(basketball_tuning)
basketball_cv_results 

# Select K with the highest mean validation accuracy.
best_k <- select_best(basketball_tuning, metric = "accuracy")
best_k

# Fit the selected workflow using the full training set.
basketball_final_fit <- basketball_workflow |>
    finalize_workflow(best_k) |>
    fit(data = basketball_train)

# Generate predictions for the test set.
basketball_predictions <- predict(
    basketball_final_fit,
    new_data = basketball_test
) |>
    bind_cols(basketball_test)

# Calculate test accuracy.
basketball_accuracy <- basketball_predictions |>
    accuracy(truth = tourney_finish, estimate = .pred_class)

basketball_accuracy

# Examine correct predictions and errors for each category.
basketball_confusion <- basketball_predictions |>
    conf_mat(truth = tourney_finish, estimate = .pred_class)

# Identify the most common tournament finish in the training set.
majority_finish <- basketball_train |>
    count(tourney_finish, sort = TRUE) |>
    slice(1) |>
    pull(tourney_finish)

# Calculate baseline accuracy on the same test set.
baseline_accuracy <- mean(
    basketball_test$tourney_finish == majority_finish
)

# Compare KNN accuracy with baseline accuracy.
basketball_comparison <- tibble(
    model = c("KNN", "Majority-class baseline"),
    test_accuracy = c(
        basketball_accuracy$.estimate,
        baseline_accuracy
    )
)

Task 6.1: Discuss your findings (10 points)¶

In 1 to 2 paragraphs (approx. 300 words or less):

  • Summarize what you found from the analysis in Part 5, in relation to your research question of interest.
  • The data science workflow is an iterative process. Discuss if at any point you had to adjust your analysis plan based on the results.
  • Discuss whether this is what you expected, or if anything was surprising.
  • Discuss the impact of the results, and what future questions this could lead to.

KNN archived 55.26% test accuracy, compared with 47.61% for the baseline. This suggests that seed and conference win percentage help predict tournament finish. I kept the original analysis plan, but I was suprised that 50 second-round losses were predicted as first-round losses. A follow-up could test whether adding conference win percentage improves predictions compared with using seed alone.
